samples.scenario: Prediction target period: from 2023-10-29 to 2024-01-14. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On October 13, 2023, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) and the Biden-Harris Administration announced $7 billion in funding to launch seven Regional Clean Hydrogen Hubs (H2Hubs) across the nation. This initiative, funded by the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, is designed to accelerate the commercial-scale deployment of low-cost, clean hydrogen. The initial Funding Opportunity Announcement for the program was issued in September 2022. The seven selected hubs are expected to catalyze over $40 billion in private investment, aiming to collectively produce three million metric tons of clean hydrogen annually, which is nearly a third of the U.S. production target for 2030. The hubs will reduce carbon emissions by 25 million metric tons annually from end-uses and create tens of thousands of jobs. The selected hubs include the Appalachian, California, Gulf Coast, Heartland, Mid-Atlantic, Midwest, and Pacific Northwest hubs. Production methods across the hubs will be diverse, including green hydrogen from renewables, blue hydrogen from natural gas with carbon capture, and pink hydrogen from nuclear power. Following the announcement, the selected hubs will enter into award negotiations with the DOE. <2> On September 28, 2023, New York Governor Kathy Hochul announced that the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Loan Programs Office (LPO) and the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA) signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU). This partnership aims to accelerate the commercialization and deployment of clean energy technologies by leveraging federal and state resources to streamline financing for large-scale renewable projects. The collaboration establishes a process for reviewing applications for LPO financing from utility-scale solar, onshore, and offshore wind projects in New York. This initiative supports New York's goal of obtaining 70% of its electricity from renewable sources by 2030 and is expected to provide alternative financing options for clean energy projects, potentially saving state ratepayers billions of dollars. <3> In conjunction with the inaugural White House Summit on Building Climate Resilient Communities held on September 28, 2023, the Biden-Harris Administration released the first-ever National Climate Resilience Framework. This framework establishes a national vision, guiding principles, and six core objectives for resilience-related activities and investments by the federal government and its partners to protect communities from the escalating impacts of climate change. The summit brought together representatives from over 25 states, territories, and Tribal Nations to emphasize community-driven, locally-tailored strategies for climate adaptation and to underscore the administration's commitment to reducing greenhouse gas emissions and managing climate threats. The framework aims to align and guide investments, embedding climate resilience into national planning and management. <4> The U.S. Departments of the Treasury and Energy, along with the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), announced on September 27, 2023, that applications for the Low-Income Communities Bonus Credit Program would open on October 19, 2023. This program, established by the Inflation Reduction Act, is designed to promote clean energy investments in underserved areas by providing a 10 or 20 percent boost to the investment tax credit for qualified wind and solar projects. The 10-point increase applies to facilities in low-income communities or on Tribal lands, while the 20-point increase is for projects that are part of a qualified low-income residential building or a qualified low-income economic benefit project. There was significant interest in the first year, with applications for the 2023 program being accepted from October 19, 2023. <5> On September 19, 2023, the U.S. Department of the Treasury published a set of nine voluntary "Principles for Net-Zero Financing & Investment." These principles are designed to guide private sector financial institutions that have made net-zero commitments, promoting consistency and credibility in their transition plans. The guidance focuses on best practices for developing and implementing these commitments, particularly concerning Scope 3 financed and facilitated greenhouse gas emissions. Key recommendations include aligning net-zero commitments with the goal of limiting global average temperature increase to 1.5°C, developing a clear transition plan with credible metrics and targets, and engaging with clients and portfolio companies to support their own transitions. The Treasury's announcement coincided with a pledge of $340 million from philanthropic organizations to support the development of research and data to help financial institutions with their net-zero goals. The release of these principles was welcomed by the Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero (GFANZ), which noted that the guidance reinforces the importance of credible and comprehensive transition plans. <6> In September 2023, the U.S. Department of the Treasury issued a set of voluntary principles for net-zero financing and investment. Published on September 19, 2023, the nine principles are designed to offer guidance to private sector financial institutions that have committed to net-zero emissions. The Treasury's stated goal is to affirm the importance of credible commitments and to encourage consistency, credibility, and transparency for financial institutions implementing their net-zero goals. The principles advise that these commitments should align with the objective of limiting the global average temperature increase to 1.5 degrees Celsius and should be supported by detailed transition plans with clear metrics and targets. This initiative represents the first time a major U.S. government agency has provided such guidance to the financial sector concerning net-zero transition plans. The release coincided with announcements from non-governmental organizations, including a $340 million philanthropic commitment to support the development of data, research, and technology to aid these institutional efforts.

[9, 11] The facility utilizes a novel process where limestone is heated to produce a calcium oxide powder, which is then spread on trays to absorb, or 'capture,' CO2 from the atmosphere. [9, 11] The captured CO2 is then sequestered, with one pathway being injection into concrete. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> January 2024 was the 10th-wettest January on record for the contiguous U.S., with precipitation totaling 3.18 inches, which is 0.87 inches above average. The national average temperature for the month was 31.8°F, 1.6°F above the 20th-century average. A notable event occurred from January 14-18, when an arctic air mass brought record-breaking cold, setting nearly 2,500 new daily minimum temperature records from the Northwest to the Lower Mississippi Valley. Later in the month, from January 22-25, parts of Texas and Louisiana experienced heavy rainfall that resulted in life-threatening floods. <2> On January 31, 2024, NOAA's Climate Prediction Center (CPC) issued its climate outlook for February 2024, which was published on February 1, 2024. [1] The forecast indicated a high probability of above-average temperatures for much of the northern half of the United States. [1] The highest chances for a warmer-than-average month, with probabilities exceeding 70%, were centered in the Northern Plains. [1] The outlook also favored wetter-than-average conditions across large portions of the southern, central, and southeastern U.S. [1] <3> On January 30, 2024, a coalition of business and industry associations, led by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the California Chamber of Commerce, filed a lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California against the California Air Resources Board (CARB). [2, 8] Other plaintiffs include the American Farm Bureau Federation, Los Angeles County Business Federation, Central Valley Business Federation, and the Western Growers Association. [2, 6] The lawsuit challenges the constitutionality of two recently enacted California climate disclosure laws, Senate Bill 253 (SB 253) and Senate Bill 261 (SB 261). [2, 4] The plaintiffs allege that these laws, which mandate broad reporting of greenhouse gas emissions and climate-related financial risks, violate the First Amendment by compelling speech. [4, 6] The suit also claims the laws overstep California's authority and are preempted by federal law under the Supremacy Clause and the dormant Commerce Clause, which grants Congress the power to regulate interstate commerce. [2, 4] <4> On January 26, 2024, the Biden administration announced a temporary pause on pending approvals for new liquefied natural gas (LNG) export projects to countries without a free trade agreement with the U.S. [1, 3, 7] This decision, influenced by sustained pressure from climate activists who have labeled the projects 'climate bombs', requires the Department of Energy to conduct an updated analysis of the environmental, economic, and national security impacts of such exports. [1, 5, 9, 10] The move was seen as a significant victory for environmental groups and young activists who had been campaigning against the expansion of fossil fuel infrastructure. [1, 4, 11] While the pause will not affect currently operating projects or those already under construction, it could delay decisions on nearly a dozen proposed facilities until after the 2025 election. [1, 7] The administration stated the pause sees the climate crisis as the "existential threat of our time," but also made assurances that exceptions could be made for national security emergencies and that the ability to supply allies would not be impacted. [5, 6, 10] <5> In a final report released on January 8, 2024, NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) confirmed that the United States experienced a record-breaking 28 individual weather and climate disasters in 2023, each causing at least one billion dollars in damages. [1] This figure surpasses the previous record of 22 such events, which occurred in 2020. [1, 2] The total cost of these 28 disasters was at least $92.9 billion, although this figure may increase as costs from a December East Coast storm are fully calculated. [1, 4] The disasters in 2023, which included 17 severe storm/hail events, four flooding events, two tropical cyclones, two tornado outbreaks, one wildfire, one drought and heatwave, and one winter storm, resulted in 492 direct and indirect fatalities. [1, 4] The costliest single event was the Southern/Midwestern Drought and Heat Wave, which accounted for $14.5 billion of the total. [1] Interim reports during 2023 tracked the rising number of disasters, with the record being officially broken by September 2023. [5, 7] <6> The United States experienced a record-breaking 28 separate billion-dollar weather and climate disasters during 2023, surpassing the previous record of 22 such events in 2020. [1, 2] While the record was already broken by October 2023 with 24 events, the final tally for the year was even higher. [3] The total cost of these 28 disasters was at least $92.9 billion. [1, 2] The events caused a minimum of 492 direct or indirect fatalities. [1, 5] The disasters included 17 severe storm/hail events, four flooding events, two tropical cyclones (including Hurricane Idalia), two tornado outbreaks, one winter storm/cold wave, one drought/heatwave, and one wildfire event, which devastated Lahaina, Hawaii. [1, 5] The costliest single event was the Southern/Midwestern drought and heatwave, which alone accounted for $14.5 billion in damages. [1] <7> In a landmark decision on August 14, 2023, a Montana judge ruled in the Held v. Montana case that the state had infringed upon the constitutional rights of young people to a 'clean and healthful environment' by failing to consider the climate-warming impacts of fossil fuel projects. This historic ruling is now serving as a precedent for other youth-led climate lawsuits nationwide. Notably, it is cited in Genesis B. v. United States Environmental Protection Agency, a new case filed on December 10, 2023, by 18 young Californians against the federal government. The Genesis lawsuit argues that the EPA has intentionally permitted dangerous levels of climate pollution, thereby discriminating against children and violating their constitutional right to life. <8> In a significant milestone for the climate movement, the Global Fossil Fuel Divestment Movement announced in December 2023 that over 1,600 institutions, with combined assets exceeding $40.6 trillion, have committed to divesting from fossil fuels. This announcement, made shortly after the COP28 conference, underscores a growing momentum to shift finances away from fossil fuels as a strategy to combat climate change. The number of participating institutions, which includes universities, pension funds, and governments, saw a substantial increase of 120 organizations holding a combined $1.4 trillion in assets in less than two years. Notable commitments in 2023 came from entities such as the Church of England, New York University, and the largest private pension fund in the Netherlands. The movement highlights a decade of organizing and is seen by supporters as a powerful demonstration of grassroots impact on financial and environmental policy. <9> On December 14, 2023, the U.S. Treasury Department's Financial Stability Oversight Council (FSOC) released its 2023 annual report, which highlighted the significant and increasing costs of climate-related financial risks to the U.S. economy and financial system. The report identifies climate change as one of 14 key financial stability vulnerabilities for 2023. It notes that more frequent and severe climate-related events are imposing substantial costs on the public and the economy, with these costs expected to rise. The council emphasized the intersection of physical risk, real estate, and the insurance market, pointing to recent instances of insurers withdrawing homeowners' coverage in states like California and Florida as a potential threat to mortgage and housing markets. The report recommends continued collaboration among federal and state agencies to develop and refine indicators for assessing climate-related financial risks in banking, insurance, and financial markets. For the first time, the council also identified the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in financial services as an emerging vulnerability.

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> In a 7-2 decision on June 20, 2025, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that fuel producers have legal standing to challenge the Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) Clean Air Act preemption waiver for California's Advanced Clean Cars I (ACC I) program. The ruling, authored by Justice Brett Kavanaugh, reverses a decision from the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals which had dismissed the producers' lawsuit. The court found that the fuel producers' claims of financial harm due to reduced gasoline demand were plausible enough to grant them the ability to sue. This decision does not rule on the merits of the ACC I program itself, which sets stringent limits on vehicle greenhouse gas emissions and mandates an increasing percentage of zero-emission vehicles through 2025. The case is now remanded back to the D.C. Circuit for further review on its merits. <2> On June 11, 2025, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), under Administrator Lee Zeldin, proposed a rule to repeal all Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emissions standards for fossil fuel-fired power plants. The proposal introduces a significant reinterpretation of the Clean Air Act, suggesting that Section 111 requires the agency to first issue a "significant contribution finding" before regulating a source category. Concurrent with this reinterpretation, the EPA proposed a finding that GHG emissions from these power plants do not significantly contribute to dangerous air pollution. This action also includes repealing 2024 amendments to the Mercury and Air Toxics Standards (MATS) for coal- and oil-fired generators, reverting to 2012 standards. As an alternative, the EPA proposed a more limited repeal focusing on specific burdensome requirements, including those based on carbon capture and sequestration (CCS) technologies. <3> A report co-authored by the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Wood Mackenzie, titled "U.S. Solar Market Insight Q2 2025," confirmed a significant slowdown in the U.S. residential solar market during the first quarter of 2025. [1, 2, 3] The sector installed approximately 1.1 GW of capacity, marking a 13% decline compared to the first quarter of 2024. [1, 2, 3] The report attributes this downturn to several factors, including sustained high interest rates and economic uncertainty, which have suppressed consumer demand for large purchases. [1, 2, 3] Additionally, the industry faces headwinds from federal policy, including potential changes to tax credits and economic risks associated with tariffs. [1, 2] <4> In the first quarter of 2025, the U.S. installed 7.4 GW of new renewable energy capacity, marking the second-strongest start to a year on record, according to a report by the American Clean Power Association (ACP). This performance was slightly behind the 8.1 GW installed in the first quarter of 2024. Utility-scale solar was the leading source of new power, contributing 4.4 GW of the total additions. The report also noted that the clean power project pipeline has expanded to 184.4 GW. <5> On June 3, 2025, the Trump administration formally requested that Congress rescind $9.4 billion in previously appropriated funds, with about $8.3 billion targeting foreign assistance programs. [1, 2] This action was part of a broader initiative to cut spending on programs the administration considered wasteful or not aligned with its priorities, including global climate assistance and public broadcasting. [2] News of the administration's plan to submit the request was reported on the same day the request was sent to Congress.
